title: Games, toys and string figures

identification.basis: Roth (1902) and Anderson (1996) describe the Bloomfield games by name; the dictionary has the words for play, fun, toys, swimming, diving and laughing.

summary: **[kinkay](word:kinkay)** 'play' and **[ngujuri](word:ngujuri)** 'to play', **[nguju](word:nguju)** and **[kuya](word:kuya)** 'fun', **[nguju-wuri-y](word:nguju-wuri-y)** 'to fool around, play about, dance in a funny/playful way', **[nguku maniway](word:nguku maniway)** 'playing together', **[baki](word:baki)** 'toy', **[yajarril](word:yajarril)** 'to laugh', **[mala-kural](word:mala-kural)** 'good diver' and **[biray](word:biray)** 'grey March fly', the name of a children's game, are the dictionary's words for this page [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's 1902 bulletin on games 'from the Bloomfield (particulars of which have been forwarded to me by Miss Violet Hislop)' and from R. Hislop at the same place, and Anderson's 1996 summary, give the Kuku Yalanji games by name: 'swinging on the lawyer-cane', diving and bubble-blowing, jumping into the water 'from the greatest height', the 'March-fly' chasing game, 'string games, using fibre and human hair twines', 'toy canoes', toy boomerangs 'made from pandanus leaves', and the rolling-disc spear game played 'on a cleared space, about 12 to 16 yards long, down more or less of a slope' with a ball 'cut out from the top of a "zamia" tree' [ref:roth1902] [ref:anderson1996]. String figures, 'cratch-cradle', are 'met everywhere throughout North Queensland', played 'for hours at a time' by 'adult women and young children, of both sexes'; Roth drew figures from the lower Palmer River, Atherton, Cape Bedford and Cape Grafton, and 'some of the figures are extremely complicated', 'passing through at least 8 or 9 stages before completion' [ref:roth1902]. Add the Palmer River's own games, the Koko-minni wrestling called 'donaman' and the hide-and-seek 'koabangan' played with a goanna claw, and the toy boomerang, which 'on the (middle) Palmer River, about latitude 16 degrees — the most northerly limit at which the boomerang has so far been met with — is employed merely as a toy' [ref:roth1902]. This page is the games as things to make and play on country now, at [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) or anywhere: the string, the lawyer cane, the zamia disc, the grass-blade shooter, the toy spear; the ceremonial side that Roth sometimes brushed, the bullroarer and the didgeridoo taught at initiation, is left out of it on purpose [ref:roth1902] [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body:
**[kinkay](word:kinkay)** 'play (yalanji)' and **[ngujuri](word:ngujuri)** 'to play (yalanji) (nyungkul - kinkay)' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[nguju](word:nguju)** 'fun'; **[ngujungu](word:ngujungu)** 'for fun or in fun, pretend'; **[nguju-wuri-y](word:nguju-wuri-y)** 'to fool around, play about, dance in a funny/playful way'; **[nguku maniway](word:nguku maniway)** 'playing together'; **[kuya](word:kuya)** 'fun'; **[kuya-bungal](word:kuya-bungal)** 'make fun of, tease in fun, make a joke' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[yajarril](word:yajarril)** 'to laugh'; **[janjarriji-y](word:janjarriji-y)** 'to laugh at someone in a friendly way'; **[judal](word:judal)** 'tricking, pretending' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[baki](word:baki)** 'toy; toys with wheels. English loan word from buggy' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[karra](word:karra)** 'rope, cord, string' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[maraji](word:maraji)** and **[mariji-y](word:mariji-y)** 'swim'; **[janjil](word:janjil)** 'wash, bathe, swim'; **[mala-kural](word:mala-kural)** 'good diver'; **[ngalu-ngalu](word:ngalu-ngalu)** 'refreshed, as after a swim' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[jalamal](word:jalamal)** 'jump, hop, skip'; **[kala-jalamal](word:kala-jalamal)** 'jump over'; **[wayi-janay](word:wayi-janay)** 'jumping around because he's happy; good dancer'; **[juru-kulbaway](word:juru-kulbaway)** 'walk single file' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[biray](word:biray)** 'grey March fly', **[kamay](word:kamay)** 'yellow March fly', **[waja](word:waja)** 'march fly': Anderson writes that 'young boys and girls played a game called birray, or "March fly"' [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996]. **[kunbu](word:kunbu)** 'a big day, celebration, as a dance, race meeting or corraborree'; **[wulngku](word:wulngku)** 'song'; **[mala-burri](word:mala-burri)** 'good singer'; **[wuri](word:wuri)** 'to dance, swing; to gamble' [ref:hershberger1982].

Roth's spellings for the Bloomfield are not the dictionary's: his 'tchugari', the small one-piece spear of the disc game, and 'teripa', the bullroarer, are given here as he wrote them and not as headwords [ref:roth1902]. The Koko-minni words 'donaman' and 'koabangan' are the middle Palmer's, in Roth's spelling [ref:roth1902].

sections.heading: Roth's Bloomfield games
sections.body:
**In the water.** 'Bathing is, of course, always indulged in at any convenient creek or waterhole, and in its wake comes splashing, diving, catching, etc. One will dive either to elude being caught himself, or the better to enable him to catch others, any convenient rocks or water-bushes being utilised for purposes of eluding pursuit' [ref:roth1902]. 'Along the Bloomfield, among what may be called such aquatic sports, is one in which the individual will, with a long breath, dive under water, and, as he swims along, blow bubbles up onto the surface; others will try and excel him'; 'the Bloomfield aboriginals will also often see who can jump into the water from the greatest height, this being always done with the feet foremost (R. Hislop)' [ref:roth1902]. Anderson: 'young men held diving competitions from tree branches into the water and also held wrestling matches' [ref:anderson1996].

**On the cane.** 'At the Bloomfield, swinging on the lawyer-cane (*Calamus*) is a common pastime. The hanging creeper is cut from 2½ to 3 feet from the ground, and the children jump and run at it, or else get others to swing them: they hold on with the hands above and feet below, the knees being extended outwards (R. Hislop)' [ref:roth1902]. The [lawyer cane](entry:lawyer-cane) is the rainforest's; on the Mitchell the swing is a rope on a river gum.

**March fly.** 'Very small children at the Bloomfield play "March-fly" as follows: Shutting his (or her) eyes, the one who takes the part of the fly runs about trying to catch someone. As soon as successful, he makes an unpleasant noise (imitative of the insect's buzz) in the ear of the child caught and also gives it a pinch (indicative of the sting)' [ref:roth1902]. The [insect page](entry:insects-and-grubs) has the real fly.

**Mimicry.** 'The mimicking, by means of attitudes and movements, of various animals, birds, etc., forms an important item in the diversions with which the aboriginals will everywhere amuse themselves in their leisure hours. Emus and kangaroos can be very well imitated', the emu with 'the mimic's one arm and hand' for 'the bird's neck and head' and 'a bunch of feathers held in the other hand, to indicate the tail' [ref:roth1902]. At Cape Bedford '"Shark" is played by little children': 'the two arms are twisted one over the other' 'and represent a shark's movements in the water', and 'a boy (or girl) rushes about with her limbs in this position, trying to catch whom she can' [ref:roth1902].

**Tracks in the sand.** 'Next to "cratch-cradle" the most general perhaps of all this particular group of imitative games is the drawing of different animal- and bird-tracks, etc., in the smoothed sand, by means of the fingers, finger-nails, palms, small sticks, etc.'; 'even in the delineation of such apparently simple things as an animal's track, a good deal of art and ingenuity is brought into execution' [ref:roth1902]. It is the [tracks page](entry:tracks-and-signs) as a game, and the way children learned the prints.

**Dolls and playing house.** 'Playing at "Houses," "Grown-ups," "Marriage" etc., is in one form or another as common among black children as it is among white ones'; at Cape Bedford 'the small girls often play at the preparation and cooking of yams and other vegetables, mimicking in the process all the actions of their elders', 'forked sticks similarly constitute girls' dolls', and elsewhere 'the parents generally make miniature dilly-bags for their children to carry these dolls in' [ref:roth1902]. 'Plait-work is met with as a pastime among the boys at Cape Bedford', 'in a form imitative of the handles of the dillybags met with further north' [ref:roth1902].

**Pets.** 'Only in the case of the dingo does true domestication and training take place. The pups are caught young, brought into camp, and tied up by the leg until such time as they become reconciled to their surroundings. Sometimes a boy (on the Bloomfield) but more usually a gin is placed in charge of these animals', and 'the aboriginals appear to be very fond of their dogs, share their food with them, often speak to them as if they were intelligent beings' [ref:roth1902]. The [dingo page](entry:dingo-and-dogs) has the rest; the station's rule on dogs is on the [cattle page](entry:cattle-and-horses) [ref:kw-induction].

sections.heading: Games and the things that are not games
sections.body:
Roth himself drew a line and sometimes crossed it. Of the 'Moon' game of Cape Bedford and the Bloomfield he wrote 'I admit having my doubts as to the propriety of doing so, the general run of the thing looking suspiciously like a remnant of some ordeal or ceremonial'; of wrestling, that it 'might be originally derived from ceremonial'; and of the bullroarer and the Bloomfield's yiki-yiki, that they are 'taught at the initiation performances' [ref:roth1902]. Anderson repeats that 'instruction in how to play the pipe was given to young men during initiation, but the instrument could be openly played in public' [ref:anderson1996]. Those things, and the games Roth records that act out spirit beings, are not on this page; they belong to the families and the old people, and if any of them is to be written down it is for them to say [ref:roth1902].

What is here is the open play: water, string, sand, toys, mimicry of animals, chasing, throwing. Roth's own test is a fair one: a game 'played in public, and before women', by children, with laughter, is a game [ref:roth1902].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: A rope on a river gum over a pool, a worn bank where children jump, a smoothed patch of sand with prints drawn in it, a cleared strip on a slope with spear holes in it, a loop of string in a pocket: the signs of play are small and everywhere [ref:roth1902]. The old zamia-disc ground would have been a strip 'about 12 to 16 yards long' on a slope near camp; nothing of it survives on the ground, but the trees do, since the [zamia](entry:zamia) is still 'cut out from the top' for the ball [ref:roth1902]. A boomerang found on the Palmer side of the country is as likely a toy as a weapon, since there it 'is employed merely as a toy' [ref:roth1902].

sections.heading: Where the games are played
sections.body:
**The waterhole** is the first playground: the dive, the bubble race, the jump from the branch, the catching game among 'any convenient rocks or water-bushes' [ref:roth1902]. At [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) that is a fenced river pool in the dry, with the [freshwater crocodile](entry:freshwater-crocodile) rule that goes with it, and never the lower tidal river [ref:kw-camping] [ref:crocwise].

**The camp** is the second: string figures by the fire, 'for hours at a time'; dolls; the sand drawing; the guess game, 'another good pastime indulged in by young and old at Cape Bedford', in which 'one of the party may perhaps notice a new flower just in blossom, a bird half hidden in a bush, a tussock of grass uprooted, etc., and taking care to look in quite a contrary direction' 'will say, "What am I thinking of?"' and 'they all try to guess, one after the other, and great laughter is aroused when the right thing is mentioned' [ref:roth1902]. The [camps page](entry:camps-and-firewood) has the camp itself.

**The slope and the open ground** are the third: the rolling disc, the toy spears, the toy boomerang, the throwing sticks, the wrestling ring, 'a cleared circular space, about 8 yards in diameter' [ref:roth1902].

sections.heading: The games of the Palmer and the Gulf side
sections.body:
Roth's Koko-minni, 'the (middle) Palmer River' people, were the Western Yalanji's neighbours and kin, and their games are the closest record to [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) [ref:roth1902]. 'Wrestling has since been met with on the Palmer (KMI, donaman)'; 'bending forwards, the challenger will grip his adversary with both hands round the loins where he interlocks his fingers so as to maintain a very firm hold: the latter, with arms raised, remains passive, and in this position is lifted from off the ground on to which he is next thrown. Honours are divided so long as he touches ground with his feet'; 'there is no mutual clutching, or both combatants falling: strictly speaking, it is a throwing, rather than a wrestling, match. Only males engage in this sport: as soon as one proves himself victorious, another challenges him' [ref:roth1902]. 'Another hide-and-seek game played by the Kokominni boys is the koabangan. While all sit round in a circle with heads low and hands over their faces, an iguana-claw is hidden in the fork of a neighbouring tree: upon a signal being given, they will jump up and commence looking for it' [ref:roth1902]. The [goanna page](entry:goanna) has the claw.

**The toy boomerang.** 'While the fighting Boomerang may be employed as a toy, the implement is often constructed solely and especially for purposes of sport and amusement'; 'on the (middle) Palmer River, about latitude 16 degrees — the most northerly limit at which the boomerang has so far been met with — it is employed merely as a toy. The toy-boomerang is thrown only by men and boys, and its throwing is the only indigenous North Queensland game wherein any real attempt is made to see who is the "best" man so to speak, but even then no so-called "prize" is awarded' [ref:roth1902]. 'When thus made as a toy, and compared with a fighting boomerang, it is lighter and smaller'; 'the boomerang is said to be right or left handed not because it is necessarily thrown with the one or other hand, but because it circles to the right or left side of the thrower', and 'until its manufacture is completed, and it has been tried by experience, the blacks have told me that they cannot determine with any degree of assurance which of the two varieties it will prove to be' [ref:roth1902]. At the Bloomfield the toy boomerangs were 'made from pandanus leaves' [ref:anderson1996]. Karma Waters sits at that same latitude, 16 degrees south; it is boomerang country only as play [ref:roth1902] [ref:kw-about].

**Cape Bedford's hunting games** are the Koko-yimidir's, not Yalanji, but they show the pattern: the 'Honey-game', 'imitative of the search for honey', in which stacked hands 'represent the trunk of a tree' and 'each hand is now in turn knocked off from above down with a side-cut — the tree is being felled'; 'Catching Cockatoos', where the hands 'represent cockatoos sitting one above the other on a branch of tree' and 'the one free hand in the group of players now makes a dart at the topmost fore-finger'; the 'Duck game', in which a child with 'a long stick' plays 'a man catching duck by means of a slip-noose attached to the end of a long slender switch', and 'the other children pass round and round, bobbing underneath the stick in Indian file, when, all of a sudden, down it comes just in front of one who will thus be considered "caught"'; and 'Tortoise', where a boy 'holds out back' a short stick 'after the manner of a wommera' and his mate 'slowly raises his hands so as to get his fore-fingers on either side of the forehead' as 'the animal with flappers rising to the water-surface in answer to the "call"' [ref:roth1902]. Every one of them is a [hunting](entry:ducks-and-geese) lesson in play.

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Water games are the dry season's, when the pools are clear and low and the river is safe to be in; the wet river is for nobody [ref:kw-camping]. String and sand are all year; the toy spears are made when the grass is tall and dry, from 'light thin withes or else from grasses, reeds, and rushes, e.g., *Andropogon schoenanthus*, *Imperata* sp.', the lemon grass and the [blady grass](entry:blady-grass) [ref:roth1902]. The grass-blade shooter wants a fresh green blade of blady grass, so it is a wet-season and early-dry toy [ref:roth1902]. The zamia disc is cut when a [zamia](entry:zamia) is being taken for food anyway [ref:roth1902] [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
Every game is a school. The sand drawing teaches tracks; the honey, cockatoo, duck and tortoise games teach the hunt; the toy spear and woomera teach the throw, 'held at their lighter ends, and thrown either with the hand' 'or with the toy wommera'; the disc game teaches the moving target, with 'spears used for this special purpose' that 'are small, made in one piece, thrown with the hand'; the diving and the bubble race teach the breath that takes [turtles](entry:freshwater-turtle) and [mussels](entry:mussels) from the bottom; the string figures teach the fingers that make [nets](entry:nets) and [dilly bags](entry:dilly-bags) [ref:roth1902]. 'In those districts where shields are employed by the adults, these may be imitated on smaller scale, and often with similar ornamentation, out of convenient pieces of bark' [ref:roth1902]. Toy canoes 'were made from bark and palm leaves' at the Bloomfield, the [canoe](entry:canoes) in small [ref:anderson1996].

**The grass-blade shooter** was a hunting tool as well: 'boys, both old and young, are very expert with this toy in the way of killing such birds as small wrens, etc. On one occasion, at the Tully, I saw a boy shooting these grass-petioles at, and hitting, some weaver-birds' nests quite over 100 feet from the ground' [ref:roth1902].

**String** is the most useful toy on earth: an endless loop of **[karra](word:karra)** in the pocket is a game, a measuring line, a snare, a lashing [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1902].

sections.heading: Making and playing
sections.body:
**An endless string.** Take about a metre and a half to two metres of twine, the [string page's](entry:string-and-twine) two-ply if you have made it, or any cord, and join the ends with a small firm knot; 'with any fair length of twine, adult women and young children, of both sexes, will often amuse themselves for hours at a time. It is thus used in the form of an endless string to play the game known to us Europeans as "cratch-cradle"' [ref:roth1902]. Roth's figures are drawn 'only' as 'the finished article', and 'during the progress of manufacture such an one requires not only the hands, but even the mouth, knees, etc., to make the different loops, twists, and turns'; 'certain of the figures may be made with two endless strings', and 'to complete others again, it may be necessary to have one or even two assistants' [ref:roth1902]. The figures he recorded from this side of the country include 'two women fighting with sticks' from the '(lower) Palmer River', 'two boys carrying spears' from Atherton, and 'four boys walking in a row, holding each other's hands' from Cape Grafton; the plates are in the bulletin, and the figures themselves live in the hands of whoever still makes them [ref:roth1902]. To start any of them: the loop over both hands behind the thumbs and little fingers, the far string picked up with the index fingers, and from there every figure is a sequence of picking up and dropping; the old people's sequences are for the contribution box below.

**The grass-blade shooter.** 'A piece of "bladey" grass (e.g., *Imperata arundinacea*) is pulled, cut to a suitable length, and split from below up, on either side of the petiole, to a convenient length'; 'the cut extremity of the grass is held loosely and horizontally between the lips, while the split ends of the leaf are bent over a stick (grasped with the right) and held in the left hand. If the stick be now driven sharply forwards, the petiole is shot away, leaving the two halves of the blade behind in the left hand. Sometimes the stick is replaced by the fore-finger of the right hand' [ref:roth1902]. The [blady grass](entry:blady-grass) page has the plant.

**A toy spear and woomera.** 'Toy spears are thus made from light thin withes or else from grasses, reeds, and rushes', 'held at their lighter ends'; 'the toy wommera can be manufactured from a rush by splitting its end, removing the pith from one of the split halves, and tying the cortex in a loop round the other: the loop retains the reed-spear in position' [ref:roth1902]. The grown-up version is on the [spear page](entry:spear-and-woomera).

**The rolling disc.** Clear 'a cleared space, about 12 to 16 yards long, down more or less of a slope'; 'at the top end of this slope one of the men will, with his spear, start rolling a ball cut out from the top of a "zamia" (*Cycas*) tree: as it rolls on and on with ever-increasing momentum, his friends lining the cleared pathway will try and job it with their spears' [ref:roth1902]. Anderson: 'a small wheel (made of a log of softwood or the top of a zamia tree) was covered on the sides by red clay and beeswax and then decorated with parrot, pigeon or cockatoo feathers. This wheel was then rolled down a hill and spears were thrown at it. Men used normal spears and boys used toy spears made from dry grasstree stems' [ref:anderson1996]. 'At Butcher's Hill and elsewhere the cycad disc may be replaced by a circular piece of bark'; so can a slice of a soft log [ref:roth1902]. The [zamia](entry:zamia), the [red ochre](entry:red-ochre), the [beeswax](entry:beeswax-and-gums) and the [grass tree](entry:grass-tree) are all on their own pages.

**Toy throwing sticks**, from the west: 'a thin rounded straight stick' 'with an elongately-knobbed extremity', '12 to 20 inches in length', 'thrown from a distance of 2 or 3 yards up and against the fringe of some overhanging bushes or leafy branches', from which 'the stick shoots through the air, knob foremost, and with greater impetus' [ref:roth1902].

**A spinning top** from the coast: 'the mamandur of Cape Bedford is made by passing a small wooden splinter through a more or less flattened and circular plate of bees'-wax and spinning it like an English boy would a "tee-to-tum"', and 'this method of spinning is adopted with the calyx-cups' of the mangrove apple and other plants [ref:roth1902].

**The water games** need no making: a branch over a deep pool for the jump, feet first always; the bubble race from one bank to the other; the catching game around a snag [ref:roth1902].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
**Water.** Jump 'feet foremost', as the Bloomfield did, and only into a pool someone has checked for depth and snags that day; a river pool changes every wet [ref:roth1902]. No swimming in the lower tidal river or any water with a [saltwater crocodile](entry:saltwater-crocodile) sign, and the Crocwise rules at every pool; the [freshwater crocodile](entry:freshwater-crocodile) bites a hand that grabs it in a snag [ref:crocwise] [ref:qld-crocbio]. Someone watches the small ones from the bank, always.

**Spears and sticks.** Toy spears are held 'differently to the fighting weapon' and thrown at the disc, never at a person; the disc game has the throwers on one side of the strip [ref:roth1902]. The grass-blade shooter is for targets, not faces.

**String.** A loop of string is a toy, not a necklace: nothing around a small child's neck.

**The sun and the ground.** Play in the shade in the hot season; the [bites-and-stings page](entry:bites-and-stings) has the ants, the March flies and the ticks that come with sitting on the ground [ref:healthdirect-insect-bites].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Roth wrote of 'games introduced of late years by missionaries, settlers, and others', and the dictionary's **[baki](word:baki)**, 'toys with wheels. English loan word from buggy', and **[kunbu](word:kunbu)**, 'a big day, celebration, as a dance, race meeting or corraborree', record the same thing: football, the races, the rodeo and the station sports day are country games now [ref:roth1902] [ref:hershberger1982]. The old ones are not gone: string figures, the swimming games and the sand drawing need nothing bought, and the disc game needs a slope, a zamia and a few hours [ref:roth1902]. Which figures the Western Yalanji women made, what the Mitchell's children called the games, and what a Karma Waters sports day looks like are for the contribution box below.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: **[kinkay](word:kinkay)** 'play'; **[ngujuri](word:ngujuri)** 'to play'; **[nguju](word:nguju)** 'fun'; **[kuya](word:kuya)** 'fun'; **[ngujungu](word:ngujungu)** 'for fun, pretend'; **[nguju-wuri-y](word:nguju-wuri-y)** 'fool around'; **[nguku maniway](word:nguku maniway)** 'playing together'; **[kuya-bungal](word:kuya-bungal)** 'make fun of'; **[judal](word:judal)** 'tricking, pretending'; **[yajarril](word:yajarril)** 'laugh'; **[janjarriji-y](word:janjarriji-y)** 'laugh at in a friendly way'; **[baki](word:baki)** 'toy'; **[karra](word:karra)** 'string'; **[maraji](word:maraji)** 'swim'; **[janjil](word:janjil)** 'bathe, swim'; **[mala-kural](word:mala-kural)** 'good diver'; **[ngalu-ngalu](word:ngalu-ngalu)** 'refreshed, as after a swim'; **[jalamal](word:jalamal)** 'jump'; **[kala-jalamal](word:kala-jalamal)** 'jump over'; **[wayi-janay](word:wayi-janay)** 'jumping around because he's happy'; **[juru-kulbaway](word:juru-kulbaway)** 'walk single file'; **[biray](word:biray)** 'grey March fly'; **[kamay](word:kamay)** 'yellow March fly'; **[waja](word:waja)** 'march fly'; **[kunbu](word:kunbu)** 'big day'; **[wulngku](word:wulngku)** 'song'; **[mala-burri](word:mala-burri)** 'good singer' [ref:hershberger1982].
